claims.text: The baseline nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
A controlled thermal treatment under a mildly reducing ethanol-oxidation environment can induce moderate Pt surface enrichment in PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles.
The proposed treatment can create Pt-rich surface regions without causing macroscopic phase separation.
Changing the local surface configuration of a complex solid-solution alloy changes its distribution of adsorption energies.
Pt surface segregation in PtPdRhRuIrOs changes the adsorption-energy distribution for ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
The affected intermediates include adsorbed CO and acetaldehyde.
The adsorption-energy changes caused by Pt enrichment steer ethanol oxidation toward complete oxidation and preferential CO2 formation.
Pt surface segregation enhances electron-transfer kinetics during ethanol oxidation.
A Pt-enriched catalyst will exhibit higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the uniformly distributed baseline.
A Pt-enriched catalyst will exhibit lower onset potential and overpotential than the uniformly distributed baseline.
A Pt-enriched catalyst will produce more CO2 relative to partial oxidation products than the uniformly distributed baseline.
A Pt-enriched catalyst will have better durability during extended operation than the uniformly distributed baseline.
The hypothesized effects are limited to ambient-temperature ethanol oxidation in acidic aqueous electrolyte and direct-ethanol-fuel-cell potential windows.
Changes in pH or extreme temperature may alter adsorption energetics enough to eliminate the proposed effect.
Interactions among the constituent metals may complicate the relationship between Pt segregation, adsorption energetics, and catalytic behavior.

contradictions.description: The causal hypothesis is conditional on successful Pt surface enrichment, but the falsification rule treats failure to produce any meaningful Pt enrichment as falsification. Failure of the intervention to instantiate the mediator is a manipulation failure, not a decisive test of the mediator's effect.
